claim: Foxj1a is necessary and sufficient to specify motile cilia.
source: Foxj1a is necessary and sufficient to specify motile cilia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: Despite all left-right organizer (LRO) cells expressing foxj1a and the ciliary axonemes of these cells having dynein arms, some cilia remain immotile.
source: We found that despite all left-right organizer (LRO) cells express foxj1a and the ciliary axonemes of these cells have dynein arms, some cilia remain immotile.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations including immunofluorescence showing foxj1a expression in all KV cells and TEM showing dynein arms in all cilia, combined with live imaging showing some cilia are immotile.

claim: The decision between motile and immotile cilia is taken early in development in the Kupffer's Vesicle (KV) precursors with her12 transcription as the readout.
source: We identified that this decision is taken early in development in the Kupffer's Vesicle (KV) precursors the readout being her12 transcription.
evidence: This is supported by her12 expression analysis in DFCs at bud stage and correlation with immotile cilia numbers at later stages.

claim: Overexpression of either her12 or Notch intracellular domain (NICD) increases the number of immotile cilia at the expense of motile cilia.
source: We demonstrate that overexpression of either her12 or Notch intracellular domain (NICD) increases the number of immotile cilia at the expense of motile cilia, and leads to an accumulation of immotile cilia at the anterior half of the KV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging experiments showing increased immotile cilia percentages upon her12 or NICD overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of her12 or NICD leads to an accumulation of immotile cilia at the anterior half of the KV.
source: We demonstrate that overexpression of either her12 or Notch intracellular domain (NICD) increases the number of immotile cilia at the expense of motile cilia, and leads to an accumulation of immotile cilia at the anterior half of the KV.
evidence: This is supported by 3D mapping of immotile cilia positions showing anterior accumulation in NICD OE embryos.

claim: The disruption of motile/immotile cilia ratio disrupts the normal fluid flow intensity and pattern.
source: This disrupts the normal fluid flow intensity and pattern, with consequent impact on dand5 expression pattern and left-right (L-R) axis establishment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluid flow measurements showing reduced velocity and altered pattern in her12 OE embryos.

claim: Disruption of fluid flow has consequent impact on dand5 expression pattern and left-right (L-R) axis establishment.
source: This disrupts the normal fluid flow intensity and pattern, with consequent impact on dand5 expression pattern and left-right (L-R) axis establishment.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization showing symmetric dand5 expression and organ situs analysis showing heterotaxia in her12 OE embryos.

claim: Motile cilia in the pit region of the mouse node generate a directional fluid flow (the nodal flow).
source: While motile cilia in the pit region generate a directional fluid flow (the nodal flow), the immotile cilia, present mostly in the perinodal crown cells, are thought to be able to sense it (McGrath et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McGrath et al., 2003.

claim: Immotile cilia in the mouse node, present mostly in the perinodal crown cells, are thought to be able to sense the nodal flow.
source: While motile cilia in the pit region generate a directional fluid flow (the nodal flow), the immotile cilia, present mostly in the perinodal crown cells, are thought to be able to sense it (McGrath et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McGrath et al., 2003.

claim: The sensing mechanism of immotile cilia is still unknown.
source: This sensing mechanism is still unknown and continues to deserve tentative updates in the field both using the mouse model (Delling et al., 2016) and the zebrafish model (Ferreira et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an ongoing question in the field with citations to recent work.

claim: Flow sensing leads to the activation of the channel Polycystin-2 (PKD2).
source: Whether it involves mechano- or chemosensation, or both, is still not demonstrated but it is known to lead to the activation of the channel Polycystin-2 (PKD2) (Yoshiba et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshiba et al., 2012.

claim: PKD2 is necessary for the asymmetric expression of dand5 on the right side of the mouse node.
source: This channel was elegantly shown to be necessary for the asymmetric expression of dand5 (DAN domain family, member 5) on the right side of the mouse node (Yoshiba et al., 2012) and consequently allowing the propagation of Nodal into the left Lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) (Marques et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshiba et al., 2012.

claim: PKD2 allows the propagation of Nodal into the left Lateral plate mesoderm (LPM).
source: This channel was elegantly shown to be necessary for the asymmetric expression of dand5 (DAN domain family, member 5) on the right side of the mouse node (Yoshiba et al., 2012) and consequently allowing the propagation of Nodal into the left Lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) (Marques et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marques et al., 2004.

claim: The Nodal signal is amplified via a self-enhanced lateral-inhibition system (SELI) at the left LPM.
source: This signal is amplified via a self-enhanced lateral-inhibition system (SELI) (Nakamura et al., 2006) at the left LPM, which consists in the activation of the genetic cascade Nodal-Pitx2-Lefty2 and ends with the correct formation and asymmetric positioning of the visceral organs (Nonaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2006 and Nonaka et al., 2002.

claim: The Kupffer's vesicle (KV) is the zebrafish left-right organizer.
source: In zebrafish, the left-right (L-R) axis establishment starts in a fluid-filled organ designated Kupffer's vesicle (KV) (Essner et al., 2005; Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Essner et al., 2005 and Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005.

claim: The KV is functionally homologous to the mouse node and the Xenopus gastrocoel roof plate.
source: Functionally, this organ is the homologue of other vertebrate LROs like the mouse node (Nonaka et al., 2002) and the gastrocoel roof plate in Xenopus (Schweickert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nonaka et al., 2002 and Schweickert et al., 2007.

claim: The KV originates from a cluster of cells called the dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs).
source: The KV originates from a cluster of cells, the dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs), which migrate in the forefront of the shield during gastrulation (Cooper and D'Amico, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cooper and D'Amico, 1996.

claim: DFCs migrate in the forefront of the shield during gastrulation.
source: The KV originates from a cluster of cells, the dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs), which migrate in the forefront of the shield during gastrulation (Cooper and D'Amico, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cooper and D'Amico, 1996.

claim: At the end of gastrulation, the DFCs form an ellipsoid fluid filled vesicle.
source: At the end of gastrulation, the DFCs form an ellipsoid fluid filled vesicle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: While KV lumen inflates, each cell extends one cilium towards the lumen.
source: While KV lumen inflates each cell extends one cilium towards the lumen (Amack et al., 2007; Oteíza et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Amack et al., 2007 and Oteíza et al., 2008.

claim: KV cilia produce a directional fluid flow that leads to an asymmetric dand5 gene expression.
source: As in the mouse node, the KV cilia also produce a directional fluid flow that leads to an asymmetric dand5 gene expression (Lopes et al., 2010; Sampaio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lopes et al., 2010 and Sampaio et al., 2014.

claim: KV cilia can be divided into two populations according to whether they are functionally motile or immotile.
source: Our previous work determined that KV cilia can also be divided into two populations according to whether they are functionally motile or immotile (Sampaio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work, Sampaio et al., 2014.

claim: The DeltaD zebrafish mutant (dld−/−) for Notch signalling presents an increase in the number of motile cilia in the LRO.
source: We also showed that the DeltaD zebrafish mutant (dld−/−) for Notch signalling (NS) presents an increase in the number of motile cilia in the LRO (Sampaio et al., 2014), suggesting that NS may modulate the number of motile cilia in this organ.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work, Sampaio et al., 2014.

claim: GALNT11 regulates the ratio between motile and immotile cilia in the Xenopus' LRO.
source: Equivalently, Boskovski et al. reported that GALNT11, an N-acetylgalactosamine type O-glycosylation enzyme needed to activate NS, regulates the ratio between motile and immotile cilia in the Xenopus' LRO, where less NS also increased the number of motile cilia (Boskovski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boskovski et al., 2013.

claim: Changing the ratio between motile and immotile cilia causes downstream defects in L-R patterning of pitx2c and in correct heart looping in Xenopus embryos.
source: The authors showed that changing the ratio between motile and immotile cilia caused downstream defects in L-R patterning of the laterality marker pitx2c (paired-like homeodomain 2), and in the correct heart looping of Xenopus embryos (Boskovski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boskovski et al., 2013.

claim: Foxj1a has been established as the motile cilia master regulator in the KV cells.
source: The transcription factor Forkhead box J1a (Foxj1a) has been established as the motile cilia master regulator in the KV cells (Stubbs et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stubbs et al., 2008 and Yu et al., 2008.

claim: Without Foxj1a, cilia do not form, altering the expression of L-R markers and randomizing organ situs.
source: Without it cilia do not form, altering the expression of L-R markers and randomizing organ situs (Tian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tian et al., 2009.

claim: Foxj1a transcription initiates during gastrulation in the DFCs.
source: Its transcription initiates during gastrulation in the DFCs, and Foxj1a is responsible for the transcriptional activation of several motility genes, such as dnah7 (Choksi et al., 2014) and dnah9 (axonemal heavy chain dyneins that mediate the movement of cilia by hydrolysing ATP) (Yu et al., 2008; Choksi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2008 and Choksi et al., 2014.

claim: Foxj1a is responsible for the transcriptional activation of several motility genes, such as dnah7 and dnah9.
source: Its transcription initiates during gastrulation in the DFCs, and Foxj1a is responsible for the transcriptional activation of several motility genes, such as dnah7 (Choksi et al., 2014) and dnah9 (axonemal heavy chain dyneins that mediate the movement of cilia by hydrolysing ATP) (Yu et al., 2008; Choksi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2008 and Choksi et al., 2014.

claim: At 3 somites stage, the vast majority of cilia were immotile.
source: The results showed that at 3 ss, the vast majority of cilia were immotile (Figure 1D) and cilia distribution and KV cell shape were homogeneous (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, F, and G from live imaging experiments.

claim: Between 3 and 5 somites stage, the highest rate of increase in the percentage of motile cilia was observed.
source: Between 3 and 5 ss, we observed the highest rate of increase in the percentage of motile cilia (Figure 1D, F–K), which then tended to stabilize at 6–8 ss (Figure 1D, L–O).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and related panels from time-lapse imaging.

claim: The percentage of motile cilia tended to stabilize at 6–8 somites stage.
source: Between 3 and 5 ss, we observed the highest rate of increase in the percentage of motile cilia (Figure 1D, F–K), which then tended to stabilize at 6–8 ss (Figure 1D, L–O).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and related panels from time-lapse imaging.

claim: 79 ± 7% of cilia transitioned from immotile at 3 ss to motile at 8 ss.
source: We found that 79 ± 7% of cilia transitioned from immotile at 3 ss to motile at 8 ss (Figure 1E), while 16 ± 8% of cilia never became motile during the time-window of the assay (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by tracking data shown in Figure 1E from time-lapse experiments.

claim: 16 ± 8% of cilia never became motile during the time-window from 3 to 8 somites stage.
source: We found that 79 ± 7% of cilia transitioned from immotile at 3 ss to motile at 8 ss (Figure 1E), while 16 ± 8% of cilia never became motile during the time-window of the assay (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by tracking data shown in Figure 1E from time-lapse experiments.

claim: At 3–4 somites stage, there is a complete absence of directional fluid flow.
source: Therefore, at 3–4 ss we observed a complete absence of directional fluid flow (Figure 2A and C; 5 embryos; 258 tracks), with the native particles presenting what seemed to be Brownian motion (2.32 ± 0.95 μm s−1; Figure 2—video 1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fluid flow measurements shown in Figure 2A-C from particle tracking experiments.

claim: At 3–4 somites stage, native particles present Brownian motion with velocity 2.32 ± 0.95 μm s−1.
source: Therefore, at 3–4 ss we observed a complete absence of directional fluid flow (Figure 2A and C; 5 embryos; 258 tracks), with the native particles presenting what seemed to be Brownian motion (2.32 ± 0.95 μm s−1; Figure 2—video 1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fluid flow velocity measurements from particle tracking.

claim: At 5–6 somites stage, a weak directional fluid flow begins to be observed with velocity 6.61 ± 3.26 μm s−1.
source: As development progressed and the number of beating cilia increased (5 ss – 63 ± 23%; 6 ss – 76 ± 8%; Figure 1D), we began to observe a weak directional fluid flow at 5–6 ss (6.61 ± 3.26 μm s−1; Figure 2G), which at this time was still homogeneous throughout the KV (Figure 2—video 2; Figure 2E – G; 5 embryos; 309 tracks).
evidence: This is supported by fluid flow measurements shown in Figure 2E-G from particle tracking experiments.

claim: At 7–8 somites stage, the directional fluid flow acquired its characteristic velocity (9.81 ± 5.36 μm s−1) and heterogeneous pattern.
source: Finally, at 7–8 ss, when the number of beating cilia began to stabilize (8 ss – 83 ± 6%; Figure 1D), the directional fluid flow acquired its characteristic velocity (9.81 ± 5.36 μm s−1) and heterogeneous pattern (Figure 2—video 3) (Sampaio et al., 2014), presenting a faster flow at the anterior-left quadrant of the KV (Figures 2I, K and 3 embryos, 128 tracks).
evidence: This is supported by fluid flow measurements shown in Figure 2I, K from particle tracking experiments.

claim: At 7–8 somites stage, the KV presents a faster flow at the anterior-left quadrant.
source: Finally, at 7–8 ss, when the number of beating cilia began to stabilize (8 ss – 83 ± 6%; Figure 1D), the directional fluid flow acquired its characteristic velocity (9.81 ± 5.36 μm s−1) and heterogeneous pattern (Figure 2—video 3) (Sampaio et al., 2014), presenting a faster flow at the anterior-left quadrant of the KV (Figures 2I, K and 3 embryos, 128 tracks).
evidence: This is supported by fluid flow pattern analysis shown in Figure 2I, K.

claim: The percentage of motile cilia increases throughout development, ranging from 27% at 3–4 ss to 70% at 5–6 ss to 84% at 7–8 ss.
source: Again, we observed an increase in the percentage of motile cilia throughout development, ranging from 27% at 3–4 ss (4 embryos; 48 cilia; Figure 2D), 70% at 5–6 ss (4 embryos; 63 cilia; Figure 2H) to 84% at 7–8 ss (4 embryos; 89 cilia; Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by high-speed video analysis shown in Figure 2D, H, L.

claim: Cilia beat faster as development progresses, with CBFs of 33 ± 4 Hz at 3–4 ss, 37 ± 5 Hz at 5–6 ss, and 40 ± 4 Hz at 7–8 ss.
source: The CBFs calculated were 33 ± 4 Hz (4 embryos; 8 cilia), 37 ± 5 Hz (4 embryos; 29 cilia), and 40 ± 4 Hz (4 embryos; 34 cilia) for the 3–4 ss, 5–6 ss and 7–8 ss, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cilia beat frequency measurements from high-speed video analysis.

claim: The ciliary frequency at 7–8 ss was significantly higher than at 3–4 ss.
source: The ciliary frequency at 7–8 ss was significantly higher than at 3–4 ss.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of CBF measurements.

claim: The comparative transcriptomic analysis yielded a list of 706 genes with a linear fold change in transcription higher than 2 after curation.
source: After curation, we obtained a list of 706 genes with a linear fold change (FC) in transcription higher than 2 (Table S1a in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the result of microarray analysis comparing WT and dld−/− DFCs.

claim: 18% (129 genes) of the genes in the microarray list were related to ciliogenesis.
source: The result of these intersections showed that 18% (129 genes) of the genes in our original list were related to ciliogenesis and of those, 67% (86 genes) were specifically related to motility (Table S1b in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on intersection analysis with ciliary gene databases.

claim: 67% (86 genes) of the ciliogenesis-related genes were specifically related to motility.
source: The result of these intersections showed that 18% (129 genes) of the genes in our original list were related to ciliogenesis and of those, 67% (86 genes) were specifically related to motility (Table S1b in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on intersection analysis with ciliary gene databases from motile cilia models.

claim: foxj1a was up-regulated (FC = 1.62, p value = 0.029) in the microarray.
source: Because foxj1a was up-regulated (FC = 1.62, p value = 0.029) in the microarray, we also compared our gene list with the list of Foxj1a-induced genes published by Choksi et al. (2014).
evidence: This is a direct result from the microarray analysis.

claim: The number of foxj1a-positive cells and the number of cilia present in each KV were concordant.
source: We fixed embryos at 8 ss and by immunofluorescence with an antibody against GFP and another against acetylated alpha-tubulin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E; Video 3), we confirmed that the number of foxj1a-positive cells and the number of cilia present in each KV were concordant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F; p=0.9479, 7 embryos, 514 cells, 513 cilia).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: foxj1a:GFP was present in all KV cells despite the fact that some cells have immotile cilia throughout development.
source: This experiment showed that foxj1a:GFP was present in all KV cells despite the fact that some cells have immotile cilia throughout development.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis of the foxj1a:GFP reporter line.

claim: foxj1a mRNA is strongly expressed in the DFCs at bud stage.
source: We confirmed that, as reported before by Yu et al. (2008) foxj1a mRNA is strongly expressed in the DFCs at bud stage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is confirmed by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation to Yu et al., 2008.

claim: The early foxj1a expression at bud stage is not yet seen with the foxj1a:GFP minimum promoter.
source: However, this early expression is not yet seen with the foxj1a:GFP minimum promoter described by Caron et al. (2012) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Caron et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison of in situ hybridization and reporter expression patterns.

claim: At 8 ss the mRNA expression of foxj1a is no longer observed in the KV, while it is detectable in the pronephros and neural tube.
source: On the other hand, at 8 ss the mRNA expression of foxj1a is no longer observed in the KV, while it is detectable in the pronephros and neural tube, but the reporter shows GFP in all KV cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C–E, respectively).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization and reporter expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The foxj1a:GFP promoter is not faithfully representing the foxj1a gene expression along time.
source: So, we must conclude that this promoter is not faithfully representing the foxj1a gene expression along time.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between mRNA expression and reporter expression patterns.

claim: The foxj1a:GFP observed at 8 ss is due to a delayed reporter and/or GFP perdurance.
source: Altogether these experiments suggest that foxj1a is expressed in all DFCs and that the foxj1a:GFP observed at 8 ss is due to a delayed reporter and/or GFP perdurance.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal mismatch between mRNA and reporter expression.

claim: The foxj1a mRNA staining closely matches the sox17:GFP labelling.
source: However, by comparing the foxj1a in situs with another reporter line for DFCs, the sox17:GFP reporter, we showed that the foxj1a mRNA staining closely matches the sox17:GFP labelling (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: When NS is reduced, the number of immotile cilia in the KV decreased significantly from 20 ± 5% in controls to 12 ± 4% in dld−/−;dlc−/− mutants.
source: The live imaging analysis showed that when NS is reduced, the number of immotile cilia in the KV decreased significantly from 20 ± 5% in controls to 12 ± 4% in dld−/−;dlc−/− mutants (Figure 4F; 24 embryos, 1047 total cilia in control; 7 embryos, 304 total cilia in dld−/−;dlc−/− mutants).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When NS is increased, the number of immotile cilia increased from 20 ± 5% in controls to 31 ± 10%.
source: Conversely, when NS is increased, the number of immotile cilia increased from 20 ± 5% in controls to 31 ± 10% (Figure 4F; 8 embryos, 353 total cilia in NICD OE;).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NS levels interfered with the motile/immotile cilia ratio and not with the total number of cilia.
source: Importantly, NS levels interfered with the motile/immotile cilia ratio and not with the total number of cilia (24 embryos, 44 ± 12 cilia in Control versus 8 embryos, 44 ± 11 cilia in NICD OE,; p=0.9154) or with cilia length (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of total cilia numbers and cilia length measurements.

claim: There were no changes in the actual number of motile cilia when foxj1a was over-expressed, irrespective of the NS background.
source: So, despite the qPCR data showing a significant increase in both dnah7 and foxj1a transcription levels after foxj1a was over-expressed (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, respectively), live imaging experiments showed that there were no changes in the actual number of motile cilia when foxj1a was over-expressed, irrespective of the NS background (Figure 4F; nine embryos, 380 total cilia in Foxj1a OE; eight embryos, 368 total cilia in dld−/−;dlc−/− mutants + Foxj1 a OE; eight embryos, 347 total cilia in NICD OE +Foxj1 a OE).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4F comparing different Foxj1a overexpression conditions.

claim: The failure of Foxj1a OE to increase the number of motile cilia, and specifically the failure in rescuing the loss of motile cilia in the NICD OE embryos strongly suggests that the KV cells are already committed to a certain motility fate.
source: We conclude that the failure of Foxj1a OE to increase the number of motile cilia, and specifically the failure in rescuing the loss of motile cilia in the NICD OE embryos (Figure 4F) strongly suggests that the KV cells are already committed to a certain motility fate.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NS modulates the functional decision of cilia motility downstream of Foxj1a function.
source: We propose NS modulates such functional decision downstream of Foxj1a function.
evidence: This is proposed based on the inability of Foxj1a overexpression to rescue the NICD phenotype.

claim: Overexpressing Foxj1a did not cause a significant change in motile cilia CBF.
source: However, by overexpressing Foxj1a, we observed no significant change in motile cilia CBF (WT = 37.27 ± 7.202 Hz, Foxj1a OE = 36.30 ± 6.877 Hz; p=0.4990; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by CBF measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In dld−/− mutants, there was no increase in CBF.
source: This experiment also agreed with the fact that in dld−/− mutants, we did not observe an increase in CBF (Sampaio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Overexpression of Her12 caused a significant increase in the percentage of immotile cilia from 20% in controls to 27%.
source: We observed a significant increase in the percentage of immotile cilia from 20% in controls to 27% (Figures 4F, 9 embryos, 305 total cilia), recapitulating the results observed in the NICD OE assay (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Dnal1 was present in both motile and immotile KV cilia.
source: Our results showed that Dnal1 was present in both motile and immotile KV cilia (Figure 4G – R; six embryos; compare K, N, Q with L, O, R).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging of dnal1-mCherry construct shown in Figure 4G-R.

claim: In the sample of cilia positive for dnal1-mCherry, 72% were motile cilia and 28% were immotile cilia.
source: In the sample of cilia positive for dnal1-mCherry, we saw 72% of motile cilia and 28% of immotile cilia.
evidence: This is based on quantification of dnal1-mCherry positive cilia.

claim: The ratio of motile to immotile cilia in dnal1-mCherry expressing cells is not statistically different from controls.
source: This ratio is not statistically different from the one for the controls used in Figure 4F (p=0.17, Fisher test) meaning that the dnal1-mCherry construct did not affect the cilia motility status and that both motile and immotile cilia can express dnal1-mCherry.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of cilia ratios.

claim: Primary cilia from the tail region around the KV were all negative for dnal1-mCherry.
source: Importantly, primary cilia from the tail region around the KV were all negative for dnal1-mCherry, which shows that in a mild overexpression scenario, this construct cannot enter a primary cilium (Figure 4J,M,P).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4J, M, P.

claim: Most KV cilia have dynein arms, i.e., may have the necessary machinery to move.
source: Overall this experiment suggests that most KV cilia have dynein arms, i.e., may have the necessary machinery to move.
evidence: This is inferred from the dnal1-mCherry expression in both motile and immotile cilia.

claim: A total of 101 cilia were imaged by TEM, providing an average of 34 cilia per KV.
source: We imaged a total of 101 cilia, providing an average of 34 cilia per KV, which according to Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, represents on average a random coverage of 77% of the cilia population of each KV.
evidence: This is based on TEM sampling methodology.

claim: All cilia imaged by TEM had an ultra-structure characteristic of motile cilia.
source: Our findings demonstrated that all cilia imaged had an ultra-structure characteristic of motile cilia.
evidence: This is based on TEM analysis of cilia ultrastructure.

claim: Some cilia had a clearly visible central pair while others showed an unfocused central pair and all cilia had visible dynein arms.
source: Some cilia had a clearly visible central pair while others showed an unfocused central pair and all cilia had visible dynein arms (Figure 4U - W; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by TEM images shown in Figure 4U-W and quantified in Table 1.

claim: It is very likely that all KV cilia are equipped with motility apparatus.
source: So, we conclude that it is very likely that all KV cilia are equipped with motility apparatus.
evidence: This is concluded from TEM analysis showing dynein arms in all sampled cilia.

claim: In the control situation, 29 ± 8% of the DFCs were her12 positive.
source: Importantly, we showed that in the control situation 29 ± 8% of the DFCs were her12 positive (Figure 5M; 9 embryos) which represent 10% more than the percentage of immotile cilia detected at 8 ss in the motility assay (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: In NICD OE embryos, there was a significant increase of 14% in the percentage of her12 positive DFCs.
source: We found a significant increase of 14% in the percentage of her12 positive DFCs (Figure 5M; from 30 to 44 ± 11%; 9 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: her12 positive cells were preferentially located at the posterior half of the DFC 3-dimensional cluster.
source: Additionally, we noticed that these cells were preferentially located at the posterior half of the DFC 3-dimensional cluster (Figure 5N; 40 ± 5% and 60 ± 5% for the anterior and the posterior halves, respectively; 9 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 5N.

claim: When NICD is over-expressed, her12 positive cells became homogeneously distributed in both the anterior and posterior halves of the DFC cluster.
source: When NICD is over-expressed, regarding cell distribution, we noticed that her12 positive cells became homogeneously distributed in both the anterior and posterior halves of the DFC cluster in contrast to the control situation (Figure 5N; 9 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 5N.

claim: When NICD was overexpressed, there was a significant accumulation of immotile cilia at the anterior part of the KV.
source: Only when NICD was overexpressed, was there a significant accumulation of immotile cilia at the anterior part of the KV (Figure 5T–V; 8 embryos; 107 cilia), thus supporting our hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by 3D mapping of immotile cilia positions shown in Figure 5T-V.

claim: In WT embryos, posterior to anterior transitions are the most common type of cell position transitions.
source: Overall, our results showed that in WT embryos, posterior to anterior transitions are the most common (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A – B, four embryos, nine cilia transitions, 19 immotile cilia tracked), further confirming our model.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse tracking data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: DeltaD protein is mainly present in the cells surrounding posteriorly, laterally and dorsally to the cluster of DFCs.
source: This assay showed that DeltaD protein is mainly present in the cells surrounding posteriorly, laterally and dorsally to the cluster of DFCs (Figure 5—video 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,G and F, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: NS occurs between the DeltaD positive cells forming a crescent posteriorly to the DFCs and notch1b positive DFCs.
source: We thus conclude that NS occurs between the DeltaD positive cells, forming a crescent posteriorly to the DFCs, depicted in our model in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H. notch1b positive DFCs (FC = 3.3 in Table S1a, Supplementary file 1) together with notch1a, notch2 and notch3 are also expressed in the DFCs at bud stage.
evidence: This is inferred from DeltaD localization and notch receptor expression data.

claim: her12 overexpression leads to a loss of the dorsal-anterior flow hotspot.
source: Fluid flow analysis showed that her12 overexpression leads to, not only a loss of the dorsal-anterior flow hotspot (compare Figure 6A–B with Figure 6C-D) but also a 12.5% reduction in flow velocity (Figure 6B,D; from 9.94 ± 4.47 in WT to 8.70 ± 4.26 µm s−1 in Her12 OE; 9 and 12 embryos, respectively; 533 and 521 tracks, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by fluid flow analysis shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: her12 overexpression leads to a 12.5% reduction in flow velocity.
source: Fluid flow analysis showed that her12 overexpression leads to, not only a loss of the dorsal-anterior flow hotspot (compare Figure 6A–B with Figure 6C-D) but also a 12.5% reduction in flow velocity (Figure 6B,D; from 9.94 ± 4.47 in WT to 8.70 ± 4.26 µm s−1 in Her12 OE; 9 and 12 embryos, respectively; 533 and 521 tracks, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by fluid flow velocity measurements shown in Figure 6B, D.

claim: 42% of embryos overexpressing Her12 showed a symmetric dand5 expression pattern.
source: Regarding dand5 expression pattern, it correlated with the difference in the fluid flow: in contrast to 100% of asymmetric on the right in control embryos (Figures 6E, 10 embryos), 42% of embryos overexpressing Her12 showed a symmetric expression pattern (Figures 6E, 12 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 41% of Her12 overexpressing embryos displayed heterotaxia.
source: In terms of organ situs, 41% of Her12 overexpressing embryos displayed heterotaxia (incorrect positioning of either the heart or liver; Figures 6F, 75 embryos) while 100% of the control embryos showed left heart and left liver (situs solitus; Figures 6F, 99 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by organ situs analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: There was no significant difference in cilia length between Her12 OE and control experiments.
source: To test if the observed decrease in flow speed and pattern, as well as the change in dand5 expression pattern and organ situs were not due to a change in cilia length we measured the cilia length from 7 KVs upon Her12 OE (without arl13b-GFP). The results showed that there was no significant difference between treated and control experiments (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by cilia length measurements shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Her12 OE leads to an increase in the number of immotile cilia at the anterior KV halves.
source: In order to check if the Her12 OE really recapitulated the NICD effect leading to an increase in the anterior immotile cilia, we then counted the motile and immotile cilia that were present on the Anterior-Posterior halves of each KV. These results confirmed an increase in the number of immotile cilia at the anterior KV halves upon Her12 overexpression (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: The change in location of immotile cilia and its accumulation at the anterior half of the KV had a significant effect in fluid flow dynamics, impacting on dand5 expression pattern and consequently in organ situs.
source: Altogether, we demonstrated that the change in location of immotile cilia and its accumulation at the anterior half of the KV had a significant effect in fluid flow dynamics, impacting on dand5 expression pattern and consequently in organ situs.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined results of cilia distribution, flow analysis, dand5 expression, and organ situs.

claim: The average number of cilia in a KV is 44 ± 12.
source: By performing live imaging in a two-photon microscope we could establish that the average number of cilia in a KV is 44 ± 12 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B; 1047 cilia in 24 embryos), which according with our previous predictions (Sampaio et al., 2014)is more than sufficient to create a robust fluid flow at 8 ss, even accounting for the observed 20% of immotile cilia in WT embryos.
evidence: This is based on quantification from live imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A minimum of 30 cilia is necessary for a robust fluid flow showing anterior-left hotspots at 8 ss.
source: The changes in fluid flow velocity as the number of motile cilia increased are in line with our previous predictions (Sampaio et al., 2014), which dictated that a minimum of 30 cilia is necessary for a robust fluid flow showing anterior-left hotspots at 8 ss (Smith et al., 2014; Montenegro-Johnson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors and others.

claim: The number of motile cilia was not affected by overexpressing foxj1a.
source: Contrary to our expectations, we showed that the number of motile cilia was not affected by overexpressing foxj1a.
evidence: This is based on live imaging experiments comparing foxj1a OE to controls.

claim: The balance between motile and immotile cilia is regulated by NS, similarly to what was reported in the Xenopus LRO.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that the balance between motile and immotile cilia is regulated by NS, similarly to what was reported in the Xenopus LRO (Boskovski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' data and comparison to cited work.

claim: The authors did not detect the same interaction between NS and foxj1a as suggested by Boskovski et al. (2013).
source: However we did not detect the same interaction between NS and foxj1a as suggested by Boskovski et al. (2013).
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental results differing from cited work.

claim: NS affects Gemc1/MCIDAS, which are required for Foxj1 expression and multiciliated cell fate determination.
source: It is also known that NS affects Gemc1/MCIDAS, which are required for Foxj1 expression and multiciliated cell fate determination (Kyrousi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kyrousi et al., 2015.

claim: NS indirectly regulates the pattern of multicilliated cells in the epidermis of Xenopus laevis embryos and in the human airway epithelium by the process of lateral inhibition.
source: In this context NS indirectly regulates the pattern of multicilliated cells in the epidermis of Xenopus laevis embryos and in the human airway epithelium, by the process of lateral inhibition (Deblandre et al., 1999; Marcet et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deblandre et al., 1999 and Marcet et al., 2011a.

claim: The differentiation and patterning of multiciliated cells and monociliated principal cells in zebrafish pronephric ducts is determined by a NS-dependent lateral inhibition mechanism.
source: Additionally, the epithelia of the pronephric ducts from zebrafish embryos also present two types of cells, a multiciliated cell and a monociliated principal cell. Their differentiation and patterning is also determined by a NS-dependent lateral inhibition mechanism (Ma and Jiang, 2007; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma and Jiang, 2007 and Liu et al., 2007.

claim: Foxj1a overexpression fails to rescue the immotile cilia number caused by the up-regulation of NS provided by NICD injection.
source: We were the first to show in the present study that foxj1a overexpression fails to rescue the immotile cilia number caused by the up-regulation of NS provided by NICD injection (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Foxj1a acts early to specify all KV cilia as motile cilia and then Notch signalling triggers an immotility switch.
source: We propose here that Foxj1a acts early to specify all KV cilia as motile cilia and then Notch signalling triggers an immotility switch.
evidence: This is proposed based on the combined evidence from expression studies, rescue experiments, and ultrastructural analysis.

claim: The authors were the first to sample the whole KV by transmitted electron microscopy and to provide a high number of analysed cilia.
source: As far as we are aware we were the first to sample the whole KV by transmitted electron microscopy and to provide a high number of analysed cilia.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: NS is acting downstream of Foxj1a to establish immotility.
source: Collectively, our results show that NS is acting downstream of Foxj1a to establish immotility.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental evidence.

claim: her12 transcription proved a faithful NS readout in the KV cell precursors.
source: In our hands her12 transcription proved a faithful NS readout in the KV cell precursors.
evidence: This is based on her12 expression responding to NS manipulations.

claim: DeltaD binds to Notch1a to activate transcription of her12.
source: We thus suggest that DeltaD binds to Notch1a [as suggested by Shankaran et al. (2007)] to activate transcription of her12.
evidence: This is suggested based on the authors' data and citation to Shankaran et al., 2007.

claim: Her12 perhaps together with other factors, restricts the number of motile cilia, most likely by inhibiting the early transcription of a yet unknown crucial motility switch.
source: Subsequently, Her12 perhaps together with other factors, restricts the number of motile cilia, most likely by inhibiting the early transcription of a yet unknown crucial motility switch.
evidence: This is speculated based on Her12's role as a transcriptional repressor and its effects on cilia motility.

claim: Overexpressing her12 resulted in a significant increase of immotile cilia in the anterior half of the KV, thereby softening the difference between anterior and posterior flow speed.
source: Here we determined that overexpressing her12 resulted in a significant increase of immotile cilia in the anterior half of the KV, thereby softening the difference between anterior and posterior flow speed (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution and flow analysis shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: The results on motile/immotile cilia ratio were uncoupled from the cilia length defects that Notch signalling causes.
source: We would like to emphasize that the results presented here on motile/immotile cilia ratio were uncoupled from the cilia length defects that Notch signalling causes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Figure 6G) (Lopes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cilia length measurements and citation to Lopes et al., 2010.

claim: Ferreira et al. (2017) determined a considerably smaller percentage of immotile cilia in the zebrafish LRO.
source: A recent work by Ferreira et al. (2017) determined a considerably smaller percentage of immotile cilia in the zebrafish LRO.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to another study.

claim: The discrepancy in immotile cilia percentage between this study and Ferreira et al. can be explained by the different pixel dwell times used during acquisition.
source: This discrepancy can be explained by the different pixel dwell times used during acquisition in the two different studies.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for methodological differences.

claim: The pixel dwell time was ten times higher in this study compared to Ferreira et al.
source: The pixel dwell time was ten times higher in our study, meaning that while we spent 22.4 microseconds per pixel, Ferreira et al. spent 2.4 microseconds.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological difference between studies.

claim: A longer pixel dwell time is crucial because it will produce a very sharp image of the trajectory of each cilium, reconstituting the beating pattern of a motile cilium or showing a very bright stiff cilium for an immotile cilium.
source: Therefore, a longer pixel dwell time is crucial because it will produce a very sharp image of the trajectory of each cilium, reconstituting the beating pattern of a motile cilium (Figure 1B), or in the case of an immotile cilium it will show a very bright stiff cilium (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is explained as a methodological advantage with reference to Figure 1B and C.

claim: According to Ferreira et al. some embryos at 8 somites show 0% of immotile cilia which contrasts with the 20% detected in this study by two independent methods.
source: According to Ferreira et al. some embryos at 8 somites show 0% of immotile cilia which contrasts with the 20% we have detected by two independent methods.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison highlighting the difference in results.

claim: The authors cannot agree with Ferreira et al.'s conclusion that refutes the immotile cilia mechanosensory hypothesis.
source: Finally, the reason why immotile cilia detection method is important to be clarified is because Ferreira et al. (2017) refute the immotile cilia mechanosensory hypothesis based on their results. We therefore cannot agree with such conclusion.
evidence: This is stated as disagreement with another study's interpretation.

claim: Based on this study's results and Ferreira et al.'s theory, from 5 to 6 somite stage, there are enough immotile cilia per KV to be able to sense flow.
source: In fact, according to Ferreira et al. own theory for mechanosensation to work, we would need at least 3 immotile cilia on each LR side to discern noise from productive flow. Therefore based on our results and their theory, we can conclude that from 5 to 6 somite stage, we have enough immotile cilia per KV to be able to sense flow (13 cilia at 5 ss and 9 cilia at 8 ss, on average, which is more than 3 cilia on each side).
evidence: This is inferred by applying Ferreira et al.'s criteria to this study's data.

claim: The mechanosensing hypothesis cannot be excluded until demonstration of a chemosensing or mixed mechanism emerges.
source: So, overall we propose that the mechanosensing hypothesis cannot be excluded until demonstration of a chemosensing or mixed mechanism emerges.
evidence: This is proposed as a conclusion about the state of the field.

claim: The balance between motile and immotile LRO cilia in zebrafish needs to be tightly regulated for the proper establishment of the L-R axis, by producing a robust, and most importantly, a heterogeneous patterned fluid flow.
source: Taken together it is possible to conclude that the balance between motile and immotile LRO cilia in zebrafish needs to be tightly regulated for the proper establishment of the L-R axis, by producing a robust, and most importantly, a heterogeneous patterned fluid flow.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental evidence showing effects on flow and laterality.

claim: In opposition to the mouse embryo, the fish LRO is very sensitive to motile cilia number and localization, most likely because of the different topographies of these two LROs.
source: We would like to stress that in opposition to the mouse embryo (Shinohara et al., 2012) the fish LRO is very sensitive to motile cilia number and localization, most likely because of the different topographies of these two LROs.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for species differences with citation to Shinohara et al., 2012.

claim: In mouse all motile cilia are on the floor of the node contributing to the effective flow, whereas in zebrafish ventral pole cilia are antagonistic to the desired flow.
source: Whereas in mouse all motile cilia are on the floor of the node contributing to the effective flow, in zebrafish ventral pole cilia are antagonistic to the desired flow (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between mouse and zebrafish with citation to Smith et al., 2014.
